section.title: The Twelve Sent, the Five Thousand, and Peter's Confession
section.sectionRationale: This movement brings the Galilean ministry to its climax. Jesus sends the Twelve out with His own power and authority, which stirs Herod to wonder who Jesus is. Jesus then feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish. On the far side of that abundance comes the turning point of Luke's Gospel: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ of God, and Jesus at once foretells His suffering and calls all who would follow to take up the cross daily.
section.thesis: The question 'Who is this?' is answered here: Jesus is the Christ of God, who provides for His people out of nothing, yet whose messiahship runs through rejection, death, and resurrection, so that following Him means denying self and taking up the cross daily to save one's life by losing it for His sake.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the sending of the Twelve; Herod's perplexity over Jesus; the feeding of the five thousand; Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ of God; and the first passion prediction with the call to take up the cross.

units.label: The Twelve sent out
units.note: power and authority to preach and heal

verses.text: Then Jesus called the Twelve together and gave them {{dynamis|power}} and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases.
And He sent them out to proclaim the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God and to heal the sick.
“Take nothing for the journey,” He told them, “no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic.
Whatever house you enter, stay there until you leave that area.
If anyone does not welcome you, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that town, as a testimony against them.”
So they set out and went from village to village, preaching the gospel and healing people everywhere.

units.label: Herod's perplexity
units.note: who is this man I hear such things about

verses.text: When Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, he was perplexed. For some were saying that John had risen from the dead,
others that Elijah had appeared, and still others that a prophet of old had arisen.
“I beheaded John,” Herod said, “but who is this man I hear such things about?” And he kept trying to see Jesus.

units.label: The feeding of the five thousand
units.note: you give them something to eat

verses.text: Then the apostles returned and reported to Jesus all that they had done. Taking them away privately, He withdrew to a town called Bethsaida.
But the crowds found out and followed Him. He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and He healed those who needed healing.

As the day neared its end, the Twelve came to Jesus and said, “Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding villages and countryside for lodging and provisions. For we are in a desolate place here.”
But Jesus told them, “You give them something to eat.” “We have only five loaves of bread and two fish,” they answered, “unless we go and buy food for all these people.”
(There were about five thousand men.) He told His disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.”
They did so, and everyone was seated.
Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, Jesus spoke a blessing and broke them. Then He gave them to the disciples to set before the people.
They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
One day as Jesus was praying in private and the disciples were with Him, He questioned them: “Who do the crowds say I am?”
They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, that a prophet of old has arisen.”
“But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “The {{christos|Christ}} of God.”

units.label: The passion foretold and the call to the cross
units.note: deny yourself, take up your cross daily

verses.text: Jesus strictly warned them not to tell this to anyone.
“The Son of Man must suffer many things,” He said. “He must be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.”
Then Jesus said to all of them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his {{stauros|cross}} daily and follow Me.
For whoever wants to save his {{psyche|life}} will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will save it.
What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet lose or forfeit his very self?
If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when He comes in His glory and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
But I tell you truly, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God.”

dynamis.gloss: Power, might, effective force to accomplish something. Jesus gives the Twelve His own power over demons and disease, so that their mission carries not their strength but His. The same divine power fed the crowd and healed the sick; the apostles go out as bearers of a power that is entirely His gift.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, the reign of God breaking into the world. The Twelve are sent to proclaim it, Jesus teaches the crowd about it, and He promises that some will see it come with power. The kingdom advances through preaching, healing, and provision, and supremely through the suffering and vindication of the King Himself.

christos.gloss: Christ, the Anointed One, the Greek for Messiah. It names the long-awaited King and Deliverer promised through the prophets. Peter's confession, 'The Christ of God,' is the turning point of the Gospel, yet Jesus immediately redefines what that title means: not immediate triumph, but a Messiah who must suffer, be killed, and rise.

stauros.gloss: Cross, the Roman instrument of execution carried by the condemned to the place of death. To take up one's cross daily is to embrace death to self and readiness to suffer for Jesus. The image is shocking on Jesus' lips before His own crucifixion, marking discipleship as a daily following of the crucified Christ.

psyche.gloss: Life, soul, the very self. Jesus turns the word on its edge: whoever grasps to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses it for His sake will save it. To clutch at self is to forfeit the true self; to surrender it to Christ is to find it. The whole person is at stake in following Him.

basic.context: Jesus gives the Twelve His own power and authority and sends them out to preach the kingdom and heal, traveling light and depending on God. Their mission spreads Jesus' fame so widely that Herod, who had beheaded John, is unsettled and keeps trying to see Him. When the apostles return, Jesus withdraws, but the crowds follow, and He feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. Then, after praying alone, He asks the disciples who people say He is, and who they say He is. Peter answers, 'The Christ of God.' At once Jesus tells them that this Christ must suffer, be killed, and rise, and that anyone who would follow Him must deny himself and take up the cross daily.
basic.hermeneutics: The feeding and the confession belong together: Jesus provides abundantly, but His true identity is only rightly grasped when joined to His coming suffering. Peter's confession is correct, yet Jesus immediately fills the title 'Christ' with the cross, correcting every expectation of a triumphant Messiah without suffering. The call to take up the cross daily is the pattern of discipleship, not an optional extra.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus gives the Twelve His own dynamis, power, and sends them to proclaim the basileia, the kingdom. Peter confesses Him as the christos, the Anointed One of God, and Jesus at once speaks of the stauros, the cross: His own, and the one every follower must take up daily, losing his psyche, his life, to save it.
basic.typology: Jesus feeding the multitude in a desolate place recalls God giving manna in the wilderness and Elisha feeding a hundred with a little, marking Jesus as the true bread who provides for His people. The Son of Man who must suffer and rise fulfills the pattern of the rejected yet vindicated servant, and the twelve baskets echo the twelve tribes gathered around Him.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Christ of God, Peter's confession the hinge of the Gospel. But He is a Messiah who must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise on the third day. He provides bread for thousands and yet walks deliberately toward His own death, and He calls His people to follow the crucified King by dying to themselves. He is both the giver of life and the one who lays down His life.
basic.god: God's kingdom advances through Jesus and through the apostles He empowers, and it is God's own power at work in their mission and in the feeding. God's plan for the Christ runs through suffering, not around it, and it is a 'must,' a divine necessity. What God asks of disciples is wholehearted, self-denying allegiance to His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 16 tells of manna in the wilderness, and 2 Kings 4 of Elisha feeding a hundred. Isaiah 53 foretells the suffering servant rejected and killed. And Luke 24 shows the risen Christ opening the Scriptures on how the Messiah had to suffer and enter His glory.
basic.oneStory: The long question of who Jesus is reaches its answer: He is the Christ of God, who feeds His people out of nothing and reigns as King. Yet His crown comes by a cross, for the Messiah must suffer and rise. The story now turns toward Jerusalem, and all who would share His kingdom are called to follow Him by daily taking up the cross.

context.literary:
Luke 9:1 to 27 is organised around a question that is asked three times by three different people. Herod asks it in verse 9, 'who is this man I hear such things about?', the crowds answer it wrongly in verse 19, and Jesus puts it to the Twelve in verse 20, where Peter gives the right answer. Everything before verse 18 prepares the question, and everything after it answers the next question, what kind of Christ this is.

The frame is a mission and a feast. The Twelve are sent out in verses 1 to 6 and return in verse 10, and the feeding takes place on their return. Luke has placed Herod's perplexity in the middle, between the sending and the return, so the news of the apostles' work travels up to a palace and produces fear, not faith. Herod's own list of guesses, John risen, Elijah, a prophet of old, is the same list the crowds repeat in verse 19. They all recognise that something from God is happening, but they place Jesus in a category that already exists. Peter's confession breaks the category.

The feeding scene is told in careful detail. Jesus says 'You give them something to eat,' verse 13, and the disciples can only count what they lack. The action then follows a fourfold pattern, in which He took, looked up, blessed, broke and gave. Luke leaves out the walking on water and everything that Mark has between the feeding and the confession, so the confession follows the feeding directly. Luke wants the reader to hear that abundance and identity belong together.

The passion prediction in verses 22 to 27 shifts the form from narrative to address. It begins with a necessity, 'must,' and moves to a universal 'anyone,' and ends on a note of glory, 'when He comes in His glory.' This is the first of three predictions in this part of the Gospel, with Luke 9:44 and 18:31 to 33 following. The structure of the section is therefore glory, suffering, discipleship, glory, and Luke sets the transfiguration, the next passage, straight after to confirm the last word.
context.historical:
A mission by twelve men carries a symbolic weight that Jewish hearers would have felt. Israel had twelve tribes, and the appointment of twelve, Luke 6:13, signalled that Jesus was gathering the people of God anew. Sending them out with His own authority is therefore both practical and prophetic. The travel instructions in verses 3 to 5, no staff, bag, bread, money or second tunic, make the missionaries entirely dependent on the hospitality they receive, so that they carry no resources of their own and are seen to rely on God. The gesture of shaking dust off the feet is a sign that a town has rejected the message. Luke 10:11 repeats it, and Paul and Barnabas later do it at Pisidian Antioch, Acts 13:51.

Herod Antipas was tetrarch of Galilee and Perea. He had imprisoned John, Luke 3:19 to 20, and in verse 9 admits that he beheaded him. His perplexity is the response of a man who knows he has done something he cannot undo and who is told that the victim is alive, in some form. Luke records that he 'kept trying to see Jesus.' He finally gets his chance in Luke 23:8, where he wants a miracle and receives silence.

Bethsaida, where Jesus withdraws, lay on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, outside Antipas's territory, in the tetrarchy of his brother Philip. The 'desolate place' of verse 12 is a wilderness setting, and Israel's memory of God feeding His people in the wilderness is the obvious background. The five thousand 'men' were counted separately from women and children, as Matthew 14:21 notes. Barley loaves were the food of the poor, and a few dried fish were the usual accompaniment. Seating the crowd in groups of fifty would have recalled the organisation of Israel in the wilderness, Exodus 18:21, and it made distribution orderly.

For Peter's confession, 'the Christ' means the Anointed One, the long-expected king of David's line. First-century hopes were strongly political, a deliverer who would drive out Rome and restore Israel, which explains why Jesus gives a strict warning of silence. The cross was a Roman instrument of execution, familiar to any Galilean who had seen the aftermath of the revolts, so 'take up his cross daily' would have been heard as a call to the way of a condemned man.
context.canonical:
The sending of the Twelve prepares the larger mission of Acts. Luke repeats the pattern in chapter 10 with the seventy-two, and the apostles' work in Acts carries it to the ends of the earth. In Acts 1:21 to 22 the qualification for a new apostle is to have been with Jesus from John's baptism to His being taken up, which shows how central the Twelve's witness is to the church's foundation.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels, Matthew 14, Mark 6 and John 6 along with Luke. John adds the long discourse on the bread of life. The Old Testament background has two layers. Exodus 16:4 has God raining bread from heaven, and 2 Kings 4:42 to 44 has Elisha feeding a hundred with twenty loaves, 'They will eat and have some left over.' The question in Psalm 78:19, 'Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?', is answered by Jesus' act, and Psalm 132:15, 'I will satisfy her poor with bread,' is among the promises it fulfils. Luke tells the story with the same verbs, took, blessed, broke, gave, that he will later use at the Last Supper, Luke 22:19, and at Emmaus, Luke 24:30, so the readers of the Gospel are meant to see in the meal an early sign of the Eucharist.

Peter's confession appears in Matthew 16:13 to 20, where it is expanded with the words 'the Son of the living God,' and in Mark 8:27 to 30. The title 'Christ of God' returns, with a bitter edge, in Luke 23:35, where the rulers sneer at the crucified Jesus, 'if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One.' The prediction of suffering draws on Isaiah 53 and the rejection of the stone in Psalm 118:22, a verse Jesus quotes in Luke 20:17. Luke 17:25 and 24:26 repeat the same necessity. The title Son of Man comes from Daniel 7:13 to 14, where the figure receives dominion and glory, and the closing verses of this passage hold the suffering and the glory together.

The call to take up the cross is picked up by Paul, who says he has been crucified with Christ, Galatians 2:20, and by Hebrews 13:12 to 13, which urges believers to go out to Him bearing His disgrace.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke is answering the question his readers carry: what kind of Messiah is this, and what does it cost to follow Him? By setting a confession of faith between an act of generosity and a prediction of death, he shows that the right answer to who Jesus is cannot be separated from the way He chooses to save. A reader who hears only the bread and the miracles has the wrong Christ, and a reader who hears only the cross has not seen the abundance that makes the cross matter.

He also means the reader to notice the contrast between the Twelve's weakness and their authority. When Jesus tells them to feed the crowd, they see only a shortage. And yet the same men were handed 'power and authority' in verse 1 and returned with a report of success. Luke does not pretend they were consistent. He wants readers to see how a small, confused group is entrusted with the message and enabled by Christ, not by their own capacity.

Finally the passage was written for people who would face loss for following Jesus. The call to take up the cross 'daily,' a word Luke adds to the tradition, shows that he had ordinary believers in mind, not an elite of martyrs. The warnings about being ashamed of Jesus and the promise that some would see the kingdom before they died would both have encouraged a church under pressure.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter narrates specific events, a mission, a meal and a conversation, and then issues a command that is meant for every reader. The instructions to the Twelve about staffs and bags were given to that mission, and Luke records elsewhere that the instructions changed, Luke 22:35 to 36. They are not a rule that missionaries today must travel without money. What carries over is the principle of dependence on God and on those who receive the message.

The feeding describes what Jesus did for a crowd that was hungry; it does not mean that He will always multiply food in answer to need, though it assures us of His compassion and power. The disciples' command 'You give them something to eat' stands as a pattern that Christians remain responsible to meet needs, relying on Him to supply the means.

The passion prediction is description, but the call that follows in verses 23 to 26 is prescription, and it is addressed 'to all of them.' Taking up the cross is not a metaphor for putting up with minor trouble. It means a daily surrender of the self to Christ's rule, even at the cost of reputation and comfort. The text also does not promise that this loss will be rewarded with earthly gain; the reward it names is saving one's life and sharing Christ's glory.

debates.question: Why did Jesus tell the disciples not to make His messiahship known?

views.label: To prevent a false, political messianism
views.case: Popular hopes expected a Messiah who would overthrow Rome in triumph; had the crowds proclaimed Jesus 'Christ' with that meaning, it would have ignited a movement opposite to His mission, so He silences it until the cross reveals what kind of Christ He is.

views.label: Because the confession was incomplete until the cross
views.case: The title 'Christ' is true but only rightly understood in light of His suffering and resurrection; Jesus withholds public proclamation until the events that give the title its true content have taken place.

debates.bearing: Either way Jesus insists that His messiahship be defined by the cross, guarding the confession from a triumphalism that skips the suffering He came to bear.

debates.question: What did Jesus mean that some standing there would see the kingdom of God before they die?

views.label: The transfiguration and resurrection glory
views.case: Within days some of them see Jesus transfigured, a glimpse of the kingdom's glory, and soon after His resurrection and the coming of the Spirit display the kingdom's arrival with power, all within their lifetime.

views.label: The whole redemptive breaking-in of the kingdom
views.case: Others read it broadly of the kingdom's advance through Jesus' death, resurrection, ascension, and the birth of the church, all of which those present would live to witness.

debates.bearing: Both keep the promise within the hearers' lifetime and tie the kingdom's coming to the events of Jesus' death, resurrection, and the Spirit rather than to a distant future only.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 pairs dynamis and exousia, 'power and authority,' and the two words are not synonyms. Dynamis is the ability to do a thing, and exousia is the right to do it. Jesus gives the Twelve both, over 'all demons' and over diseases. It is the same pair Luke used in 4:36 of Jesus' own word, 'with authority and power He commands the unclean spirits.' The apostles act with delegated power and are not independently strong. In verse 10 they are called apostoloi, 'sent ones,' from apostellō, the verb of verse 2.

Herod's reaction in verse 7 is diēporei, 'he was thoroughly perplexed,' a compound verb of being at a loss, with no way through. The same verb describes the confusion of crowds in Acts, and here it is the reaction of a man whose conscience is troubled. His final line, 'he kept trying to see Jesus,' is in the imperfect tense, a repeated attempt.

The feeding describes a pattern of four actions. Jesus labōn, 'taking,' the loaves, looks up to heaven, eulogēsen, blessed, kateklasen, broke, and then edidou, 'kept giving,' in the imperfect tense, a verb of continual distribution. The imperfect pictures the bread passing from His hands to the disciples again and again, and the abundance appears in the giving. The leftover pieces fill twelve kophinoi, small hand baskets, one for each of the Twelve who had said they had nothing.

Peter's answer is ton christon tou theou, 'the Christ of God.' Christos is the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach, 'anointed,' and 'of God' stresses that this anointing is God's. Luke's sentence in verse 21 is epitimēsas parēngeilen, Jesus 'strictly warned' them, using the same verb of rebuke that Luke elsewhere uses of commands to unclean spirits. The silence is firm because the title can be misunderstood.

The key to the next lines is dei, 'it is necessary,' in verse 22. This verb of divine necessity occurs at the great turning points of Luke's Gospel: Jesus must be in His Father's house, 2:49, must preach the kingdom, 4:43, and must suffer, 17:25, and in 24:26 and 24:44 the risen Lord says that everything written about Him must be fulfilled. 'Rejected' is apodokimasthēnai, to be tested and found worthless, the verb of Psalm 118:22 in the Greek Old Testament, 'the stone the builders rejected.' The leaders named, elders, chief priests and scribes, are the three groups of the Sanhedrin. 'Raised' is egerthēnai, 'be raised,' the verb of resurrection used in the passive, which is the grammar of something God does.

In the call to follow, 'deny himself' is arnēsasthō heauton, from arneomai, the verb used of Peter's own denial of Jesus in Luke 22:57, and of denying Jesus before men in 12:9. The word is therefore tied to what Peter will do within a few chapters, and it makes the cost of loyalty concrete. The addition kath' hēmeran, 'daily,' belongs to Luke, as does the interplay of psychē, 'life' or 'self,' which is both what one tries to save and what one loses. The same word is behind 'his very self' in verse 25, where the one who gains the world is zēmiōtheis, 'forfeits' or suffers loss. The word stauros, 'cross,' was a Roman term for the stake or crossbeam of execution, and it could not have been heard as a metaphor in the first century.

typology.type: Manna and the table in the wilderness, Exodus 16 and Psalm 78
typology.fulfillment: God fed Israel in the wilderness with bread from heaven, Exodus 16:4, and the psalmist recalls that the people asked, 'Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?' Psalm 78:19. At Bethsaida, in a desolate place, the question is answered in a meal. The correspondence is the provision of bread for a hungry people by God's word, in groups that recall Israel's organisation in the wilderness. The escalation is that the giver is present in person, and the leftovers fill twelve baskets, more than was set out. The type falls short in that manna and loaves feed the body for a day; John 6:35 gives the deeper reading, in which Jesus is the bread of life.

typology.type: Elisha's feeding of a hundred, 2 Kings 4:42-44
typology.fulfillment: Elisha was brought twenty barley loaves and told his servant to give them to a hundred men, with the word of the LORD, 'They will eat and have some left over.' Jesus has five barley loaves and feeds five thousand men. The numbers show the escalation: the miracle of the prophet is multiplied fiftyfold in the larger work of the greater prophet. The correspondence is also in the pattern of a servant's objection answered by a command. The type falls short in that Elisha speaks on behalf of the LORD, while Jesus blesses and breaks the bread Himself, and the leftover is not a footnote but a sign of overflowing supply.

typology.type: The rejected stone and the suffering servant, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 53
typology.fulfillment: Jesus says that the Son of Man must 'be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes.' This is the language of Psalm 118:22, 'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,' which He applies to Himself in Luke 20:17, and the shape of Isaiah 53, 'despised and rejected by men,' verse 3, and 'He will see the light of life,' verse 11. The correspondence is rejection followed by vindication. The escalation is that the one rejected is also the one who bears the sin of many, Isaiah 53:12. The type is not complete in the psalm, which speaks of Israel's own king, nor in Isaiah, who does not name the servant, and it is Jesus who joins the pictures.

typology.type: The Son of Man who receives dominion, Daniel 7:13-14
typology.fulfillment: Jesus' favourite title for Himself comes from Daniel's vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds and receiving everlasting dominion. In verse 26 He speaks of the Son of Man coming 'in His glory,' which is the Danielic scene. The striking move is that in verse 22 the same Son of Man must suffer. Daniel's figure is vindicated without any mention of suffering, and Jesus fuses the glory with the cross. The correspondence is the title and the final glory; the escalation is that glory comes through death. The type is incomplete without verse 22, because Daniel gives the end of the story and Jesus supplies the road.

study.christ:
Peter's confession is the centre of the Gospel's account of who Jesus is, and Luke makes it do two jobs at once. It tells us that Jesus is the Messiah, the one the Old Testament had been waiting for. It also tells us that the title is too small until it is filled in by what Jesus says next. Immediately after Peter's answer comes 'must suffer,' and the 'must' carries the weight of Scripture and of the Father's plan. Luke does not include Peter's rebuke or Jesus' reply to him, which Mark records in 8:32 to 33. But the force of the Lord's correction of expectations is clear anyway from the strict command to silence and from the three parts of the prediction.

The way to Christ in this passage runs by provision, by identity and by pattern. By provision: He feeds a crowd that the disciples would send away. This anticipates the bread of the new covenant, and Luke's use of the same four verbs at the Last Supper shows that the evangelist saw the connection, Luke 22:19. The Lord who gives the loaves to be passed from hand to hand is the Lord who gives His own body, 'given for you.' By identity: the question 'Who do you say I am?' is the pivot, and the answer Peter gives is the truth that His life will demonstrate. By pattern: the Son of Man 'must' be rejected and killed and raised. The three verbs match the shape of the gospel Paul summarises in 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 4.

It should be noticed that the cross is not an accident that overtakes Christ. The 'must' of verse 22 says that it belongs to the purpose of God, and Luke 24:26 says the same after the resurrection: 'Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?' Isaiah 53:10 says that it was 'the LORD's will to crush Him.' Jesus does not stumble into suffering as a failed revolutionary. He walks into it as the Servant who will 'bear the sin of many.'

The call to take up the cross is no mere imitation. It is a share in what He has already done. Paul reads the matter in these terms when he says that he has been crucified with Christ, Galatians 2:20, and that 'our old self was crucified with Him,' Romans 6:6. The Christ who dies is not simply an example of self-denial but the one in whom his people die and rise. At the same time He is truly a pattern, and Hebrews 13:12 to 13 asks us to go to Him outside the camp, bearing His disgrace.

A caution is needed against forced readings. The twelve baskets are not a certain sign of the twelve tribes, though the number may have been chosen as a gentle echo, and the five loaves are not a code for the five books of Moses. The reading is firmer when it rests on the verbs and on the Old Testament texts that Jesus Himself uses. What the passage gives us is a Christ who feeds, who is confessed and who goes to the cross.
study.god:
The God of Luke 9 acts through weak instruments. He gives authority to twelve ordinary men and sends them out with no provisions. He supplies a crowd's need through the disciples' own hands, and the leftovers are collected by the same men who had said there was nothing to give. Nothing in the story suggests that the Twelve were up to the task. What is displayed is the generosity of a God who delights to work through people who have nothing of their own.

God appears as the one who provides abundantly. 'They all ate and were satisfied' is a deliberate echo of the wilderness and of the psalmist's hope that the poor would be satisfied with bread, Psalm 132:15. The fact that twelve baskets are left over shows that His giving does not run out at the point of need. It overflows. This is part of the Bible's regular picture of the Lord, who gives not just enough but more than enough, and who invites His people to share what they receive.

The chapter also shows God's plan as a plan with a necessity in it. The 'must' of verse 22 is not a prediction of bad luck, and it is not that the enemies are stronger than expected. It belongs to God's purpose. A reader might feel a tension between the God who gives bread and the God who sends His Son to die. They are the same God, and the same love. His kindness to the crowds and His willingness to give up His Son both express the identical character. The tension is resolved on Calvary, where the giver of bread becomes the bread broken.

It also shows God's way of dealing with human expectations. The crowds guessed John, Elijah and a prophet, Herod was afraid, and Peter guessed rightly but with the wrong picture. God does not conform Himself to the ideas of people, however pious. He corrects them gently, as Jesus does in verse 22, and with firmness. There is a mercy in that: the Lord prepares His people for the cross before it comes.

There is a doctrine of judgment and glory here too. Verse 26 speaks of the Son of Man coming 'in His glory and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels,' a reminder that the rejected one is also the one who will return as judge. The ashamed will be treated as they treated Him. God's justice and mercy are both on show: He provides, He suffers, and He will vindicate.

For worship, the chapter teaches the posture of the disciples who sat down in rows to be fed. Receiving is not passive, since Jesus' people are expected to pass on what they are given. And it teaches a worship of the crucified, a confession of the Christ of God that is not afraid of the cross but joins it. The God who gives bread to the hungry calls His worshippers to lose their lives for His sake, and promises that they will find them.

crossReferences.note: God promises to rain bread from heaven so that each day the people gather what they need, testing their trust. The feeding at Bethsaida shows the same God again providing in a desolate place. Where Israel received a daily portion, Jesus shows an overflow, with more left over than was set out.

Elisha multiplies twenty loaves among a hundred men and the LORD's word is that they will eat and have some left over. The disciples' objection in verse 13 has the same shape as the servant's. The Gospel account is an escalation, with five loaves feeding five thousand men.

In the wilderness the people asked whether God could prepare a table. That question, spoken in doubt, hangs over every desolate place in Israel's memory. The feeding of the five thousand answers it with a table set in the grass in orderly groups.

God promises to bless Zion with abundant provisions and satisfy her poor with bread. The poor who eat their fill in Luke 9:17 are the people this psalm promised, and the feeding becomes a sign that the promised King has come to His city.

At the Last Supper Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it, saying 'This is My body, given for you.' The same actions at the feeding show that the miracle points beyond itself to the meal in which He gives Himself. The bread given to the crowd foreshadows the bread given in death.

The rulers mock Him, 'if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One.' It is Peter's confession turned into a taunt, and it shows the cost of the title. The Christ of God is exactly the one who hangs there, and the mockery states the truth without knowing it.

The stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone. Jesus' prediction that He will be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes uses the vocabulary of this verse, which He later applies to Himself openly in Luke 20:17. Rejection and vindication belong together.

The servant is despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows. The portrait gives the Old Testament background for a Messiah who suffers, and Jesus' 'must' places Him in that figure. Peter had a king in mind. Isaiah gave a servant, and Jesus unites the two.

One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives dominion, glory and an everlasting kingdom. Jesus' title for Himself in verse 22 and the promise of coming in glory in verse 26 are drawn from this scene. The glory is certain, and the surprise is that the road to it passes through suffering.

After the resurrection Jesus asks the two on the road, 'Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?' It is the answer to the 'must' of 9:22, spoken by the risen Lord. The disciples' failure to understand in chapter 9 is overcome only when He opens the Scriptures.

Paul says he has been crucified with Christ, no longer lives, and lives by faith in the Son of God who loved him. This is the cross of verse 23 lived out from the other side. The daily taking up of the cross becomes a daily dependence on the one who was crucified in our place.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who provides in a garden full of fruit and a human race that grabs for more. The feeding at Bethsaida answers that old failure with a Lord who sits His people down in an unplanted field and fills them. Israel's wilderness story, with manna and the question whether God could set a table, finds its answer here. And the long hope of a Messiah, an anointed king from David's line, finds its answer in the words of Peter.

Yet the story that Luke tells does not match the hope as Israel had it. The prophets spoke of a king and a servant, and of a Son of Man who is given a kingdom, but few put those figures in one person. Peter's confession and Jesus' immediate correction bring them together for the first time. The Christ will be the one who is rejected, who dies and who rises. The 'must' reaches back to Genesis 3:15, where the offspring of the woman is wounded in the heel in the act of crushing the serpent, and forward to Calvary.

This is the turning point in Luke. The Galilean section ends here, and from the next verses the story heads toward Jerusalem. The disciples, who have been learning who Jesus is, are now to learn what He will do. And their own story is bound up in His, since following Him means walking the same road. The Church is the community that has taken up the cross, and its life is shaped by Christ's own pattern of loss and gain, death and life.

The rest of the Bible shows the pattern working itself out. The cross comes, the resurrection follows, and on the road to Emmaus the risen Christ explains from Moses and the prophets how the Christ had to suffer. The apostles whom He sent out here carry the message to the nations in Acts, and the bread that was given on the grass is given again at the church's table until He comes. The promise in verse 27 that some would see the kingdom before they died begins to be fulfilled in the transfiguration only a few days later, and in the resurrection and Pentecost.

The story ends where the feeding pointed all along. In Revelation the Lamb who was slain is on the throne, and His people are invited to the marriage supper, Revelation 19:9. Hunger is gone, Revelation 7:16, and the Lord who fed five thousand on a hillside is the shepherd who leads His people to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The ones who lost their lives for His sake find that they have saved them.

quiz.q: What did Jesus give the Twelve when He sent them out?

options.text: His own power and authority over demons and disease, to preach the kingdom and heal.
options.note: Luke 9:1-2 shows Jesus entrusting them with His power for their mission.

options.text: Detailed instructions to travel light and depend on hospitality.
options.note: He did give such instructions, but the heart of the sending was the power and authority He gave them.

options.text: Money and provisions for a long journey.
options.note: The opposite; He told them to take nothing for the journey.

options.text: Authority to rule over the towns they entered.
options.note: They were sent to serve, preach, and heal, not to rule over towns.

quiz.q: What happened when Jesus fed the five thousand?

options.text: He multiplied five loaves and two fish so all ate and were satisfied, with twelve baskets left over.
options.note: Luke 9:16-17 records the abundant provision from almost nothing.

options.text: He sent the crowd to buy food in the surrounding villages.
options.note: That was the disciples' suggestion, which Jesus overruled by providing Himself.

options.text: He told the disciples there was nothing they could do.
options.note: He said 'You give them something to eat,' then provided through them; He did not counsel helplessness.

options.text: He fed only the Twelve, not the crowd.
options.note: The whole crowd of about five thousand men ate and were satisfied.

quiz.q: How did Peter answer when Jesus asked, 'Who do you say I am?'

options.text: The Christ of God, the promised Anointed King.
options.note: Luke 9:20 gives Peter's confession, the turning point of the Gospel.

options.text: A great prophet like Elijah or one of the prophets of old.
options.note: That was what the crowds said; Peter's answer went further, confessing Him as the Christ.

options.text: John the Baptist raised from the dead.
options.note: This was a popular guess, even Herod's fear, not Peter's confession.

options.text: A teacher sent to reform Israel's religion.
options.note: Peter confessed far more: Jesus is the Christ of God.

quiz.q: What did Jesus teach about His messiahship right after Peter's confession?

options.text: That the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and on the third day rise.
options.note: Luke 9:22 redefines the Christ through the necessity of the cross and resurrection.

options.text: That He would soon be crowned and honored by the people.
options.note: He will be glorified, but only through suffering and death first, which Jesus stressed here.

options.text: That He would overthrow the Romans and restore Israel's kingdom.
options.note: This was the popular hope Jesus deliberately corrected by pointing to the cross.

options.text: That His identity should now be proclaimed openly everywhere.
options.note: He strictly warned them not to tell anyone yet, until the cross gave the title its meaning.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say it means to follow Him?

options.text: To deny yourself, take up your cross daily, and lose your life for His sake in order to save it.
options.note: Luke 9:23-24 sets out self-denial and daily cross-bearing as the pattern of discipleship.

options.text: To be willing to endure hardship when it happens to come.
options.note: Following Him does mean hardship, but Jesus calls for deliberate, daily self-denial, not merely passive endurance.

options.text: To admire His teaching while keeping your life as it is.
options.note: Jesus calls for losing your life for His sake, not admiration that changes nothing.

options.text: To gain the whole world and secure your own comfort.
options.note: Jesus warns that gaining the world while forfeiting your self profits nothing.

questions: Jesus sent the Twelve out depending on Him rather than on their own resources. Where is He calling you to step out in trust rather than waiting until you feel fully equipped?
The disciples saw only five loaves and two fish; Jesus saw enough to satisfy thousands. What impossible-looking need are you tempted to measure by your resources instead of bringing to Him?
Jesus asked, 'Who do you say I am?' It is not enough to know what others say. How would you answer that question today, and does your life reflect that answer?
Peter confessed the Christ, but Jesus insisted the Christ must suffer. Where are you tempted to want the glory of following Jesus without the cost of the cross?
Jesus says whoever loses his life for His sake will save it. What might it look like this week to lose your life for Him in some concrete, costly way?

translationNotes.note: 'The Christ of God' renders the Greek for the Anointed One, the Messiah, belonging to God; Matthew adds 'the Son of the living God,' but Luke's shorter form carries the same confession.
The word 'daily' is distinctive to Luke's account of this saying, stressing that cross-bearing is not a single heroic act but the ongoing shape of following Jesus.
The word rendered 'life' is psyche, which also means soul or self; the saying trades on both senses, that grasping to keep one's life forfeits the true self.
